scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Sky Dancers of Veracruz
This is Los Voladores. Pre-Hispanic to modern.
on_screen: Title card: Los Voladores · Mexico · Pre-Hispanic to modern

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The ritual originated in pre-Hispanic Mesoamerica, with evidence found in ceramics from the pre-Classic period in Nayarit.
It is believed to have been created by the Nahua, Huastec, and Otomi peoples to appease gods during a severe drought.
Following the Spanish Conquest, the ritual was suppressed, though it persisted through oral tradition and secret practice.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The ritual is a fertility rite designed to bring rain and honor the gods.
It is performed on patron saint feast days and at cultural festivals like the Cumbre Tajín.
It symbolizes the connection between the sky, earth, and underworld.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Five participants climb a 30-meter pole.
The caporal remains at the top on a platform (manzana), playing a flute and drum.
Four voladores sit on a frame (cuadro), wind ropes around the pole 13 times each, and then fall backward to descend in a spinning motion.
Watch for The Descent.

Formation: Circular descent around a vertical pole.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is performed by the caporal at the top of the pole using a one-handed flute and a small drum.
The music is categorized into 'sones', which are specific to the ritual.
Listen for the flute, drum.
The music consists of a high-pitched, melodic flute accompanied by the rhythmic beat of a small drum, played from the top of a 30-meter pole.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditional Totonac dress includes red pants, a white shirt, a cloth across the chest symbolizing blood, and a cap adorned with flowers and mirrors.
The mirrors represent the sun, and multicolored ribbons represent the rainbow.
The pole, or 'palo volador', is a 30-meter structure that serves as the central setting.

Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Jesús Arroyo Cerón was a prominent figure who trained women as voladores; he died in 2006 after a fall from a pole.
His daughter, Isabel, was one of the first women he trained.
Variations exist among the Nahua and Otomi, where there may be no dance before climbing.
The ritual is considered a continuation of ancient Mesoamerican traditions, with modern practice heavily influenced by Totonac cultural preservation efforts in Veracruz.

narration: Los Voladores is variant of Hua-hua: A related dance with less solemnity, involving a rotating frame.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The ritual is a sacred fertility rite. In some communities, women are prohibited from participating due to traditional beliefs that they bring bad luck or anger the gods.
